title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
hookLine: the gods are losing a war, and Indra's wife ties a thread of protection on his wrist
carry: raksha: a prayer of protection, and a promise
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
last: GOD TAKES THE POISON SO OTHERS LIVE.

lines: A PLAIN THREAD, A SHORT VERSE.
A WAR THE GODS WERE LOSING.
cards: Before rakhis came with glitter and cartoon characters, a protective thread was serious business.

Priests in many parts of India still go house to house on the full moon of Shravana, tying a plain thread on the wrists of the families they serve, with a short Sanskrit verse. The verse mentions a demon king.
And behind the custom, the Puranas tell of a war the gods were losing, and a wife who tied the thread.

teach.b: The story is told in the Bhavishya Purana. Indra, king of the gods, has been fighting the demons a long time, and he's losing, worn out and afraid.
His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, goes to the gods' teacher, Brihaspati, for help.
He tells her: on the full moon of Shravana, prepare a raksha, a protective thread, with the proper rites, and tie it on Indra's wrist. She does.
Indra goes back into battle with the thread on his arm, and this time he wins. Notice who ties it: a wife, not a sister. Now, the priests' verse.

teach.h: THE VERSE: AS BALI WAS BOUND.
teach.b: It remembers the demon king Bali, who was bound by Vishnu. Its sense: with the thread that bound the mighty Bali, king of the demons, I bind you; stay firm, O protection, stay firm.
So the verse asks the thread to hold the person the way Bali was held. Here's the teaching in the knot.
A raksha isn't jewelry; it's a prayer you can wear, tied on with a sacred verse. In Shachi's story, it guards the one who wears it.
In the custom families keep today, the one who wears it also takes something on: a duty to look after the one who tied it. Hindus call a duty like that dharma.

teach.h: A BLESSING GIVEN, A PROMISE ACCEPTED.
teach.b: So a rakhi carries two things at once, a blessing given and a promise accepted, and it can be tied by a wife, a priest, a sister, a cousin or a friend.

how: On Shravana Purnima, besides sisters tying rakhis on brothers, many priests tie protective threads on the wrists of the families they serve while reciting a short Sanskrit verse remembering King Bali; in some communities the same day is also when men renew their sacred thread.

games.q: your cousin ties a rakhi on your wrist. by today's teaching, what are you taking on?
o: a blessing from her, and a promise to look out for her.
protection for you only; nothing is asked of you.
games.why: in Shachi's story the raksha guards the wearer; in the family custom, the wearer also promises to protect. a prayer and a duty, tied together.

practice: Many Hindus wear a red or yellow thread tied at a puja for days afterward. If you have a thread, tie it on your wrist now; if not, picture one.

Think of someone who protected you without making a fuss: a parent who waited up, a friend who stood beside you. If you pray, say their name and ask God to protect them. If you don't, simply thank them in your mind.
Then think of one person you'd protect, and let the thread be your promise to them.

wordCard.voice: Rakhi. A thread of protection, tied in the old story by Shachi on Indra's wrist, and today by sisters, cousins, priests and friends: a blessing and a promise.

orig.note: Sanskrit rakṣā: protection, and also the protective thread itself.
